Welcome

From Classroom to Career: Evolving Skills to Lead Across Cultures

Since 2020, the Global Shared Learning Week initiative has opened virtual spaces where university communities across the Pacific Rim talk through pressing local and global issues. The APRU Open Dialogues, led with Tecnológico de Monterrey's Vice-Rectory for International Affairs, use open dialogue as a way of learning: listening deeply, speaking from experience, and understanding one another across differences.

This cohort explores the evolving role of soft skills in preparing graduates for a globalized, multicultural and fast-changing labor market. You will meet Carlos and his sister Mariana in a short story, then discuss in small international groups what it reveals about the gap between university and work, and what you can do about it.

Participants who attend the full session receive a certificate of participation, sent by email from October 29.

The two questions we will explore
  1. What perceived gaps exist between what universities teach and what the global labor market demands?
  2. What personal actions can students take to develop the soft skills needed in a future shaped by cultural diversity and technological advancement?

What you can begin to explore

This is a single two-hour dialogue, so think of it as a starting point: a chance to become more aware, try new ways of listening and speaking, and take a first step you can keep building on.

Cultural awareness

Notice how cultural differences show up at work, and hear how peers from other countries think about preparing for a global career.

Problem-solving

Explore real workplace tensions, from communication styles to expectations about time and teamwork, and try out constructive ways to respond.

Leadership & empathy

Practice listening across differences and reflect on what inclusive leadership could look like for you, balancing technical, language and people skills.

Pre-session warm-up

Four questions to think about first

These questions will get you thinking before you read the story and meet colleagues from other universities. Think about them first, then send your answers through the short form, which asks the same questions.

1 · Working in diverse teams

How equipped do you feel to work effectively in multicultural teams?

2 · Different expectations

Can you think of a time you worked or studied with someone whose idea of "on time" or "professional" was different from yours? How did you handle it?

3 · Personal or professional?

In the culture(s) you identify with, is it normal to talk about personal or family matters in a work setting? Why or why not?

4 · AI and culture

To what extent do you believe AI can help people work more effectively in multicultural settings?

Your privacy. These warm-up questions are only a way to get you thinking about the topic before the dialogue. Your answers are seen only by the organizing team and will not be shared outside it. If results are ever reported, they will be summarized in aggregate, without names or any information that could identify you, unless you give your consent.

The story

From Classroom to Career

A story grounded in workplace experience, and the shared starting point for every group. Read Part 1 before the session. Part 2 will be opened for everyone during the live dialogue.

The characters react in very different ways, on purpose. No culture in the story is "right" or "wrong". As you read, notice your own first reactions and assumptions about each character: they are a good starting point for the dialogue.

Part 1
CarlosA promising graduate leads his first multinational team, and things start to go wrong.
1 / 12

Carlos, a native Spanish speaker, graduated three years ago from a university recognized regionally for its cutting-edge and innovative character, and one that was in the process of becoming more internationally oriented. Alongside the technical competencies of his program, he had taken advantage of the language courses, local internships, and career development workshops the institution offered, though if he was honest, it was always the technical side that felt like it truly mattered. That focus paid off quickly: within months of graduating, he secured a position in a multinational technology company and moved to the capital of his country. His professional ethics, technical expertise, and command of English let him stand out, and after a couple of years he was promoted to a role coordinating a project with colleagues from three major countries around the world, all working in English as their shared language. The first virtual meetings with the multinational team ran relatively well. Getting used to each other's accents was challenging, but afterward Carlos and some colleagues often stayed on informally to chat about non-work matters and, at times, to clarify things that might have been understood differently or not completely.

Tension began when Carlos asked to reschedule a meeting to attend his nephew's baptism.* Two colleagues, Camila and Thiago, understood immediately, even celebrating the occasion. Hans and Greta, however, reacted with irritation, considering that "personal matters should not interfere with professional commitments." Soon after, punctuality became another source of conflict. Hans and Greta were always on time for virtual meetings, logging in exactly at the scheduled hour. They grew frustrated when others joined late, sometimes even Carlos. As delays accumulated, meetings dragged on. At first, they stayed connected, but eventually they began logging off once the scheduled time ended, even if important information was still being discussed.

One day, a key project deadline was missed because Hans and Greta delivered only part of their work; details had been discussed after they left the virtual meeting, and they never received the updates. That afternoon, Carlos received a direct phone call. Hans spoke bluntly: "I just need to say two things. Number one: punctuality is a basic requirement, being late shows a lack of respect. Number two: meetings must end on time; we cannot be expected to stay longer or catch up afterward." Then he abruptly hung up.

The call struck Carlos as harsh and almost offensive. He felt they were questioning his professionalism as project leader. A little flexibility on their side would have been appreciated, he thought. But ultimately they had a point: meetings were not starting or ending on time.

Shaken, Carlos called his colleague Rajesh to reinforce punctuality and ask for feedback. Rajesh surprised him: "Carlos, you keep asking the team for consensus. You are the leader, you should decide. Otherwise, we lose clarity." He also reached out to Camila and Thiago, who were often the latest to join meetings. Hoping to align expectations, Carlos asked for their perspective. They told him candidly: "Carlos, you're being too rigid. Meetings feel cold and overly formal. We need a warmer atmosphere, more space to connect as people."

Trying to respond, Carlos began the next meeting, held just after his nephew's baptism, by showing a family photo from the ceremony. He mentioned that a small "gift" from the event would arrive by mail the following week, as a token of appreciation for their flexibility. Camila and Thiago were thrilled, asking for details about the event, the parents, the food, and the music played during the celebration. After a few minutes of this warm exchange, Rajesh remarked softly: "Carlos, perhaps we should keep more focus on the agenda." Camila then asked one last question about the boy's attire, which led Carlos into a detailed explanation of the elegant suit and the family traditions behind it. At that point, Hans and Greta grew visibly irritated and cut in bluntly: "This is not the right time for personal matters, we must start the meeting now." The session went on, but with twenty minutes lost to personal discussion, the team ran out of time to finish the agenda. As usual, Hans and Greta logged off at the scheduled hour, and decided to report the incident to Carlos's leader.

The next day his boss called firmly: "Carlos, you are valuable technically, but if you don't improve your ability to adapt and lead interculturally, this project may fail… and your position is at risk." The ultimatum hit him hard. That same day, Carlos stayed extra hours at the office, reviewing every detail of the project to ensure nothing was left pending. He wanted his boss to have no complaints, at least on the technical side.

In the following days, as he walked back to his apartment, the situation replayed endlessly in his mind. At first, he thought of his university: had they really prepared him for a global, multicultural labor market, or fallen short in teaching those competencies? Then he turned his frustration toward the company and his boss: were they expecting too much, too quickly, from someone whose strengths were clearly technical?

But gradually the questions shifted inward. Some of his colleagues seemed to navigate these environments better. Were their universities more effective in developing soft skills? Or had they simply taken advantage of opportunities Carlos himself had overlooked? He began to wonder if the real issue was not only the university or the company, but the gap between what he had chosen to develop and what the global workplace now demanded.

At that moment, his phone buzzed: a message from his sister Mariana. "Hey Carlos, you haven't answered my messages, you seem absent and distant… everything okay?" Carlos decided to open up and share what he was going through.

* In some countries, a child's baptism is not only a religious rite but also a social event, often involving family gatherings, music, and shared traditions.

Dialogue session

What happens on October 28

Most of the time is spent in small international groups, each with a moderator. This is a dialogue, not a debate: the goal is to understand each other, not to win. Before the session, please read the dialogue guidelines, which everyone follows during the conversation.

  1. 0:0010 min
    Welcome and framing

    Opening words from APRU and Tec de Monterrey. Purpose of the dialogue and how it works.

  2. 0:1010 min
    Intercultural icebreaker Breakout

    Meet your group. Your moderator will explain the icebreaker activity at the start.

  3. 0:2010 min
    Topic introduction

    By Prof. Ana Carolina Vázquez Naranjo. An introduction to the dialogue theme and its goals, to help everyone start the conversation from a shared understanding.

  4. 0:3020 min
    Open dialogue, Round 1: the gap Breakout

    Based on Part 1 of the story. Trigger question: What gaps (or perceived gaps) exist between what universities teach and what the global labor market demands?

  5. 0:5010 min
    Group sharing: first insights

    All groups return to the main room to share first comments and early takeaways from Round 1. Each group chooses its reporter during the breakout; reporters, be ready to share if called on.

  6. 1:0025 min
    Open dialogue, Round 2: personal action Breakout

    Your moderator shares the code to open Part 2. First, read Part 2 of the story together, then discuss the trigger question: What personal actions can students take to develop the soft skills needed in a future shaped by cultural diversity and technological advancement?

  7. 1:2510 min
    Group sharing: conclusions

    We bring the dialogue together. A few groups share their conclusions and final takeaways, including sharing personal actions they will take forward.

  8. 1:3515 min
    Guest speaker: Benjamin Zhou

    Perspectives from a young professional on the APRU team, working in international settings.

  9. 1:5010 min
    Closing

    Thanks, next steps, and an invitation to post on the Wall of Wisdom.

  10. 2:00
    End of session

    19:00 Mexico City time.

    Exit surveyPlease complete it at the end of the session. It is anonymous and takes about 5 minutes.

Dialogue guidelines

  • Speak in the first person, from your own experience.
  • Listen attentively, especially when you disagree.
  • Assume the best intentions in every contribution.
  • Honor confidentiality: share lessons learned, not names.
  • Don't take comments personally. Focus on the ideas.
  • Respect diverse perspectives.
  • Be concise so everyone has time to speak.
  • Short answers are welcome, and it's fine to pass and listen.
Keep your camera on. Use raise-hand and reactions to signal questions or agreement. During each breakout, your group chooses one person to report back to everyone.

Times count from the start of the session (17:00 Mexico City). Total: 120 minutes.

Further reading and contacts

General references on the topics of this dialogue, listed in order of relevance. All are free to read online under Creative Commons licenses and are optional.

  1. Krumrey-Fulks, K. (2022). Intercultural Communication for the Community College (2nd ed.). Open Oregon Educational Resources. CC BY-NC-SA

    Suggested focusChapter 10, Business: how cultural dimensions such as time, hierarchy and individualism shape communication and teamwork at work.

  2. Nielsen, D., Ballantyne, E., Murad, F., & Fournier, M. Getting Ready for Work-Integrated Learning. BCcampus. CC BY-NC 4.0

    Suggested focusChapter 8, Interpersonal Skills (adaptability, emotional intelligence) and Chapter 9, Effective Communication (active listening): the soft skills that matter in the move from classroom to workplace.

  3. Carpenter, J., et al. Career and Workforce Readiness. eCampusOntario. CC BY-NC 4.0

    Suggested focusIn-Demand Skill Areas and Professional Expectations: what employers look for, with self-reflection exercises on your own skills.

This site supports the APRU Open Dialogues 7th Cohort. It is intended only for nominated participants, moderators and organizers, and is used for educational purposes.

Temporary site

The site is available only while the 7th Cohort program runs (October–November 2026). After the program ends it will be taken offline.

Please don't share or reuse

Do not copy, redistribute or reuse the story, illustrations, audio or other materials, and do not share the session code, without prior consent from the organizing team.

Respectful use

Contributions such as Wall of Wisdom posts must follow the dialogue guidelines. The organizers may remove content that is disrespectful, off-topic or shares other people's personal information.

The story of Carlos and Mariana is fictional and was created for educational purposes. While fictional, it is inspired by common intercultural communication challenges in the workplace and is grounded in intercultural communication theory and practical experience. Any resemblance to real people or organizations is coincidental. Some materials, including the illustrations, were developed with the support of AI tools.

Warm-up answers and check-ins are seen only by the organizing team and reported only in aggregate, without identifying information, unless you consent.
